---
title: "The Ten Decisions: Executive Summary"
subtitle: "A 3-Minute Brief for Specialty Food Founders"
date: "2026-01-01"
date-format: "YYYY"
---

You built this brand to $25 million. The product works. The retail relationships
are real. And somewhere in the last three years, the business became harder to run
than it should be.

Not harder in the way growth is supposed to be hard — hiring, logistics, keeping
up with demand. Harder in a quieter way. Margins that should be improving aren't.
Cash that should be accumulating isn't. Chargebacks arriving that nobody has time
to fight. Retailers growing in revenue and somehow costing more every quarter than
they used to.

This is not a product problem or a people problem. It's a data structure problem.

You've outgrown the systems that were adequate at $5M and haven't yet built the
decision infrastructure that a $25M specialty food brand requires. The cost of
that gap — across ten structural decisions that growing brands routinely make
without data — runs between **$1.4 million and $2.3 million a year.** Not
projected. Not theoretical. The gap that exists in the current business, right
now, because ten operational choices are being made blind.

---

The first five decisions are about what you have today.

Which SKUs are paying their way — and which ones are consuming production
capacity, broker attention, and warehouse space without earning back their keep.
At 50 SKUs across ten channels, you need a model to do what your gut did at 15.

Whether your product data — GTINs, item attributes, case dimensions, GS1 registry
entries — will hold up when the next retailer asks for it, or generate chargeback
notices 60 days after the onboarding from errors that have been in the catalog
for two years.

How much of the revenue you've billed has been quietly taken back in deductions
— short pays, advertising charges, compliance fees — and whether your team has a
systematic process to dispute them in the 30–60 day window before they expire
uncontested. Most brands at $25M recover about 15 cents of every dollar
deducted. Eighty-five cents stays out.

Whether operational failures are being tracked. Short-shipped orders don't just
lose revenue — the legacy system overwrites the original PO quantity with the
shipped quantity, and the cost of the gap disappears from the records. You lose
the revenue, the fill rate history, and the ability to make the case for recovery.

And whether your EDI is catching errors before shipment or paying for them in
chargebacks 30 days after the truck left the dock. A missing SSCC-18 barcode is
$100 per case. A late ASN is $500 per load. A pre-flight check catches both in
under 60 seconds.

Most brands at $25M are making all five without adequate data. Not neglected.
Invisible — because nobody built the infrastructure to surface them.

---

The next two decisions reveal whether you understand the business you actually
have.

Which channels are making you money: not which ones generate the most revenue,
but which ones return the most per dollar of broker fee, trade spend, and margin
concession. The largest channel and the most profitable channel are rarely the
same one. Operating without a per-channel contribution model means every trade
dollar goes to the account with the biggest revenue number — which is usually
also the most demanding buyer relationship and the thinnest net margin.

And why the bank account doesn't match the sales report. Revenue that looks clean
in the pipeline is losing ~13 cents of every dollar to deductions, chargebacks,
payment timing gaps, and invoice leakage before it becomes cash. No one has mapped
the full waterfall because no single system captures the journey — the invoice is
in accounting, the deductions are in a spreadsheet, the chargebacks are in the
dispute queue. The leakage is structural and knowable. It just hasn't been looked
at yet.

---

The final three decisions are about what's next.

Whether you're structurally ready when a major retailer says yes — across product
data, EDI capability, FSMA traceability, fulfillment capacity, and team readiness
— before you sign the PO, not after the first failed delivery. A Red EDI
dimension at Walmart isn't a flag in a project plan. It's 8–12 weeks of
remediation before you can ship a compliant order. A GFSI certification gap at
Whole Foods isn't a two-week fix. It's a complete launch block.

Whether you know what saying yes to that retailer actually costs you in Year 1.
Slotting fees front-load before you ship a single case. Net-60 payment terms mean
you've funded two months of inventory before seeing any cash. Trade spend and OTIF
compliance reserves are committed upfront. The 12-month P&L and cash flow model
shows you the path before you commit to it.

And whether you have the three-number weekly report that keeps all nine other
decisions from drifting back to blind: cash position, disputed AR balance, and
at-risk shelf velocity. Missing one week of attention doesn't break a business.
Missing six weeks does.

---

These ten decisions don't operate in isolation. They compound.

Fulfillment failures generate chargeback notices 45 days later. Those chargebacks
strain cash at the moment a production run needs funding. The cash gap delays the
product data cleanup that would have stopped the next round of onboarding errors.
The channel you're overinvesting in delivers the thinnest margin — but nobody
modeled it because the contribution tool doesn't exist yet. The weekly report that
would show you this loop forming was never built.

The loop doesn't break a $25M specialty food brand in a quarter. It makes the
business harder to run every quarter — until the brand that should be scaling is
treading water, winning accounts and somehow making less money every time one
calls.

---

The ten decisions aren't obscure. Every specialty food CEO knows they should be
tracking these numbers. The problem isn't awareness. It's that nobody has built the systems to
make all ten visible — simultaneously, in the same business — until someone
decides to.

That is the work. Not dashboards for their own sake. Not data as a deliverable.
The decision infrastructure that turns operational data into the ten choices
that determine whether a specialty food brand scales or stalls.
